earnings.headline: Intuit grew sales 14 percent in its last quarter and full year, but expects slower growth next year.
points: Sales (revenue) for the year rose 14 percent to $21.4 billion. The last quarter also grew 14 percent, to $4.4 billion.
Profit per share (EPS) rose 20 percent to $16.46 for the year. Its newer 'Big Bets' products grew 34 percent.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next year is sales up 9% to 10%, slower than this year's 14 percent.
Weak spots: U.S. TurboTax users fell to 39.0 million from 39.9 million. Mailchimp sales are expected flat to slightly down.
Intuit sells TurboTax (taxes), Credit Karma (credit and loans), QuickBooks (business accounting) and Mailchimp (email marketing).
Credit Karma sales rose 20 percent to $2.6 billion. TurboTax grew more slowly, up 7 percent to $5.3 billion.
It spent $5.5 billion buying back its own stock, up 96 percent. It holds $7.2 billion in cash but owes $7.7 billion in debt.
Risks they name: competition, the government doing taxes itself, keeping up with AI, hacking and fraud, and a restructuring plan.
Several headlines say the stock has been falling, including one drop of 7% before its next earnings report.
One article ties the drop to fears that a new AI finance tool could compete with TurboTax.
The next earnings report is set for November 19.

takeaways: The business grew well last year: sales and profit both rose, and it passed $20 billion in yearly sales.
Growth is expected to slow next year, and fewer people used TurboTax this year than last year.
Investors are worried AI tools could take tax customers away. Intuit says AI is central to its own plan.

earnings.headline: Coca-Cola sold more drinks, grew sales 7%, grew profit faster, and raised its own full-year forecast.
points: Sales grew 7% to $13.4 billion. People bought 5% more drinks worldwide, led by India, China, Mexico and Brazil.
Operating income (profit from running the business) grew 12%. Earnings per share (profit per share) rose 8% to $0.93.
They raised their full-year guidance (their own forecast), but the forecast numbers were not in the text we read.
Weak spots: North America drink volume was flat, sports drinks fell 3%, and they lost market share in Europe, Middle East & Africa.
They own big drink brands like Coca-Cola, Sprite, fairlife and Powerade, sold in more than 200 countries via bottling partners.
In 2025, $28.8 billion of their sales came from outside the United States, so swings in the dollar can lift or cut results.
Named risks: new laws on plastic, water use and climate could raise their costs or force them to change some recipes.
They warn some brand and investment values may need write-downs (impairment charges) if future cash forecasts fall short.
Many headlines say the stock hit record highs after a 95% run.
Some writers worry the price is high: Barron's says its valuation (price compared to profits) is the highest in 25 years.
Writers disagree on what comes next. These are opinion pieces, not official company news.

takeaways: The quarter was mostly good: more drinks sold, higher sales, and wider profit margins than a year ago.
Not every part grew: North America volume was flat, sports drinks slipped, and they lost share in one big region.
A weaker dollar helped results this quarter. The company's own report warns that currency swings can also hurt.

earnings.headline: Sales more than doubled to $159.0 million and the loss shrank to $5.2 million, but Angel still lost money.
points: Sales (revenue) were $159.0 million, up 107.7% from a year ago. Guild memberships brought in $115.6 million of that.
Still losing money, but less: net loss was $5.2 million, down from $38.5 million a year earlier.
Their own forecast (guidance) is unchanged: an Adjusted EBITDA loss (a cleaned-up loss) of less than $25 million for 2026.
Paying members hit 2.94 million. But cash fell to $45.6 million from $63.3 million a year ago, and they owe $75.5 million in notes.
They earn from Guild memberships, a cut of movie ticket sales, licensing shows to Amazon, Apple and Netflix, and merchandise.
At the end of 2025 they had about 2.0 million paying members and held about 303.1 bitcoins as a company savings asset.
They raised cash by selling new shares: about $55.0 million in September 2025, plus a plan to sell up to $150,000,000 more.
Risks they name: a history of losses, hits are hard to predict, movies need big upfront marketing, and a long patent lawsuit.
Headlines say Q3 showed a loss, but sales beat what analysts expected.
The stock was added to the Russell 2000 and 3000 indexes (big lists of US companies that many funds follow).

takeaways: Fast growth: sales and paying members are rising quickly, and the cost to win members is a smaller share of sales than a year ago.
Not profitable yet: the company still lost money this quarter and expects a loss for the full year.
Watch cash and shares: cash is lower than a year ago, it owes money, and selling new shares can shrink each owner's slice.

earnings.headline: Palantir's sales grew 96% from a year ago to $2.313 billion, and it raised its own forecast for the full year.
points: Sales (revenue) were $2.313 billion, up 96% from a year ago. It was the first quarter ever above $2 billion.
Profit (GAAP net income) was $1.128 billion, a 49% margin, so it kept about half of each sales dollar as profit.
Guidance (their own forecast): Q4 sales of $2.649 - $2.653 billion, and full-year 2026 sales of $8.530 - $8.534 billion.
Weaker spot: new contracts signed (TCV) were $2.918 billion, up only 6% from a year ago, far slower than sales growth.
They rent out software (Foundry, Gotham, Apollo, AIP) that helps governments and companies use their data and AI.
In 2025, sales were $4.5 billion, up 56% from $2.9 billion in 2024. Customers grew from 711 to 954.
Risk they name: many contracts can be canceled "for convenience," so future deal value is not certain to turn into sales.
Other named risks: wars, interest rates, currency swings and tariffs could hurt them or their customers.
Many headlines ask why the stock keeps falling even though the business is growing fast.
One headline cites a 25% drop from an October high. Others debate whether the price is too high for the growth.

takeaways: The business is growing very fast and is now very profitable, with $10.4 billion in cash and U.S. Treasury securities.
New contract signings grew much more slowly than sales. That is worth watching.
A fast-growing company is not the same as a cheap stock. The headlines show the share price fell anyway.

earnings.headline: Broadcom's sales hit $29.6 billion this quarter, up 86 percent from a year ago, mostly from chips used for AI.
points: Sales (revenue) were $29.6 billion, up 86 percent. AI chip sales alone were $16.7 billion, up 221% from a year ago.
Profit per share (EPS) under standard accounting rules was $2.68, up from $0.85 in the same quarter last year.
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: about $34.8 billion in sales, up 93 percent. It is only an estimate and could miss.
'Adjusted' profit of $20.1 billion leaves out real costs, like stock paid to workers. Software sales grew much slower than chips.
They make money two ways: computer chips (a lot of them for AI data centers) and business software, like VMware's cloud tools.
In fiscal 2025 the business brought in $27,537 million of cash and paid $11,142 million to shareholders as dividends.
They also spent $2,450 million buying back their own stock that year.
Risks they name: losing big customers, AI demand cooling, relying on a few suppliers, and a large amount of debt to repay.
The stock has swung hard lately: one headline says it fell 22% in a month, another says it jumped 18.2% in a week.
One report says well-known investor David Tepper sold all his Broadcom shares last quarter.
Several headlines tie Broadcom's moves to other AI chip makers, like Nvidia.

takeaways: Broadcom is growing very fast right now, mostly because big tech firms are buying its AI chips.
That growth leans on a small group of huge customers; if they cut spending, sales could fall.
The company pays a $0.65 per share dividend each quarter, but its stock price has been swinging a lot.

earnings.headline: McDonald's grew profit and worldwide sales this quarter, but U.S. same-store sales dipped slightly.
points: Sales at all restaurants rose 4% to over $38 billion. McDonald's own revenue (sales plus franchise fees) rose only 1%.
Profit rose 9% to $2,486 million. Profit per share was $3.51, up 10%, helped by higher other income and fewer shares.
U.S. same-store sales fell 0.2%: fewer visits, offset by bigger orders. China and France were weak spots.
No new forecast (guidance) given. CEO says U.S. improved through the quarter after value-menu moves. Dividend up 4% to $1.93.
Several headlines argue the stock looks pricey versus estimates of fair value. These are opinions, not facts.
Business news: value menu tests, an Uber delivery expansion, and marketing to gamers on Discord.
One report asks if McDonald's can protect its profit margins if food costs keep rising in 2027.

takeaways: Profit is still growing, helped mostly by franchise fees and other income, not by more customers.
In the U.S., fewer people visited and bigger orders covered the gap. The value-menu push aims to bring visits back.
The annual report text pulled here had no business or risk sections, so this summary covers the latest quarter only.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 11% to $2.8 billion, but profit fell sharply because of big one-time costs from buying other companies.
points: Sales (revenue) rose 11% to $2.8 billion. Newer drugs grew 49% to $1.26 billion, helped by drugs bought with Apellis.
Older multiple sclerosis (MS) drug sales fell 13% to $919 million, and copycat drug (biosimilar) sales fell 16%.
Adjusted profit per share fell 46% to $2.62. By official (GAAP) rules they lost money, mostly from $284 million in deal costs.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 profit per share went up at the low end: now $12.20 to $13.00, from $12.00 to $13.00.
They sell medicines for brain and nerve diseases like MS, SMA and ALS, and share Alzheimer's drug LEQEMBI with Eisai.
Cash and investments rose to about $4.2 billion at the end of 2025, up from about $2.4 billion a year earlier.
Cash from everyday business fell 23.3% in 2025, partly from higher tax payments and payments for deals.
Risks they name: cheap generic copies of TECFIDERA and a rival copy of TYSABRI keep cutting sales; tariffs add uncertainty.
Headlines focus on new two-year data saying their early Alzheimer's drug diranersen slowed decline.
Eisai and Biogen shared three-year real-world LEQEMBI data showing slower Alzheimer's progression.
Results from two big lupus drug trials are expected in the first half of December 2026.

takeaways: The company is growing again: newer drugs are selling fast enough to make up for older MS drugs losing ground.
Profit took a hit this quarter, mostly from one-time costs of buying companies, and total debt is about $7.7 billion.
Several big drug trial results are due over the next 12 months. They could help or hurt; nothing is certain.

earnings.headline: Sales jumped and the company raised its own yearly forecast, but its official operating profit shrank sharply.
points: Revenue (sales) grew 39% from a year ago to $3.44 billion, which the CEO called a record first quarter.
Operating income (official profit from running the business) fell to $96 million, from $309 million a year ago.
Net income (profit after all costs) rose to $482 million, or $0.57 per share, from $334 million a year ago.
Guidance (their own forecast) was raised: full-year sales of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, up 26% to 27%.
They sell cybersecurity: firewalls, cloud and AI protection, and tools that guard logins, mostly as subscriptions.
Big change: after buying CyberArk, they say the business got much bigger and that brought new risks and rivals.
Risks they name: tough competition, including cloud giants and AI firms that offer their own security tools.
Other risks: a hack or a flaw in their own products could hurt their name, and past growth may not continue.
Headlines say they agreed to buy AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion.
Several stories say the stock rose after results topped what Wall Street analysts expected.
Other stories tie demand to AI-driven cyberattacks becoming a bigger threat.

takeaways: Sales and signed future contracts are growing fast, and the company expects more growth this year.
Official operating profit shrank a lot even as sales grew, which means costs grew faster than sales.
They keep buying other companies (CyberArk, and now plans for Applied Compute). Deals like these can pay off or cause problems.

earnings.headline: Record quarter: sales rose 65% to $10.2 billion, topping the company's own forecast.
points: Sales (money from customers) were $10.2 billion, up 65%. Without buyouts and currency effects, growth was 37%.
Profit per share (EPS) was $0.79, up 61%. New orders hit a record $12.2 billion, more than they shipped (1.19:1).
Their own forecast (guidance) for next quarter: sales of $10.3 to $10.5 billion. For all of 2026: $36.9 billion to $37.1 billion.
Caution: they're paying about $1.6 billion for four companies, partly with borrowed money (debt). Forecasts may not come true.
They make connectors, cables, antennas and sensors that link electronics together, built in about 40 countries.
Biggest unit, Communications Solutions, was 52% of 2025 sales. Harsh Environment was 26%. Interconnect and Sensor was 22%.
They estimate their whole market was worth about $500 billion in 2025.
The full risk list wasn't in the text we read. The company warns that results could differ a lot from its forecasts.
Several articles debate whether the stock price is already too high for the company's growth.
One article asks what happens to Amphenol if spending on AI data centers slows down.
One headline says the stock fell 3.41% on Nov 16.

takeaways: Sales and profit grew fast this quarter and beat the company's own forecast.
They're sharing cash with owners: a 20% bigger dividend and a new $4 billion plan to buy back their own shares.
Much of the growth comes from data-center demand and buyouts partly paid with debt. If that demand slows, growth could slow too.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 39% to $782.5 million, their fastest growth in nearly four years, but the official loss got bigger and margins slipped.
points: Sales (revenue) were $782.5 million, up 39% from a year ago. The CEO called it their best quarter ever.
Official (GAAP) loss grew to $34.1 million from $1.3 million. Adjusted profit, which skips stock pay and some other costs, was $143.7 million.
Gross margin (what's left of each sales dollar after direct costs) slipped to 71.2% from 74.0% a year ago.
Their own forecast (guidance): $845.0 to $846.0 million in sales next quarter, and $2,963.0 to $2,964.0 million for the full year.
They make money mostly from subscriptions. Businesses pay monthly or yearly to use their network for security and speed.
Sales were $2,167.9 million in 2025, up from $1,669.6 million in 2024.
They have lost money every year since they began. The loss for 2025 was $102.3 million.
Risks they name include slower growth, tariffs raising equipment costs, and a weak economy cutting customer spending.
Most headlines cover the stock jumping after results, citing faster sales growth and a raised full-year forecast.
Some stories link the growth to customers using Cloudflare's AI platform to build apps.
Not all one way: one headline asks why the stock fell on a Tuesday after the big run-up.

takeaways: Sales are growing fast, up 39% in a year, and the company's own forecast for the year went up.
It still loses money under official accounting, and that loss got bigger this quarter.
The company plans to cut part of its workforce as it leans harder on AI. That brings one-time costs.

earnings.headline: Joby raised its sales forecast and made progress on FAA approval, but it still spends far more cash than it brings in.
points: Sales (revenue) were $55 million in Q3 2026, mostly from Blade, its passenger flight service, which flew 44,000+ people.
No profit number is given. They expect to use $385 million to $415 million of cash in the second half of 2026.
Their own forecast (guidance) for 2026 sales rose 15%, to $135 million to $140 million.
Surprise: its J208 plane flew itself across the U.S., and Air Force contracts grew to ~$37 million. It plans to buy Resonant Sciences.
Joby is building an electric air taxi for a pilot and up to four passengers. It plans to run rides, sell aircraft and do defense work.
In August 2025 Joby bought Blade, a passenger air charter service in New York and Southern Europe.
Joby has lost money every year since 2009. Its total past losses (accumulated deficit) were $2,785.6 million at the end of 2025.
Biggest named risks: FAA approval could be late or never come, government shutdowns, crowded airspace, and rivals getting there first.
Headlines say the stock is still down 56% in 2026, even though it rose after the Q3 results.
Several stories focus on how much cash Joby is burning and say its biggest hurdle is still ahead.
Other articles guess how far the stock could rise or fall. These are opinions, not company facts.

takeaways: Joby does not sell air taxi rides yet. Almost all of its sales today come from Blade.
It still spends far more than it earns, but it has $2.2 billion in cash and short-term investments to fund the work.
The key thing to watch is FAA approval. It is in the fifth and final stage, and the company warns it could take longer than planned.

earnings.headline: Match Group says Q3 met its own targets and Tinder's daily users grew again in September, but the release gives no sales or profit figures.
points: Tinder's daily users grew vs. a year ago in September, the first time in three and a half years.
Hinge grew users, sales, and paying users by double digits vs. last year.
Tinder's sales are not growing yet. The company says it hopes to turn better user trends into sales growth in 2027.
They cut the number of shares by 4% in a year and 10% since early 2025, and will pay a $0.20 per share dividend on January 21, 2027.
Most money comes from people paying directly in apps like Tinder and Hinge (subscriptions and extras). Ads bring in some too.
Apple and Google take fees on in-app purchases, a big cost. The company names cutting these fees as a risk it may not achieve.
They renamed their main profit measure to "Adjusted EBITDA" (profit before some costs). The number itself did not change.
They carry debt, with $450 million due December 15, 2027. Named risks include losing users, competition, and cyberattacks.
Headlines discuss the Q3 results and a raised guidance (the company's own forecast).
A company director bought 2,500 shares, according to one report.
The finance chief will speak at UBS and Nasdaq London conferences in December.

takeaways: Tinder, the biggest app, is showing early signs of getting more users again, but its sales have not caught up yet.
Hinge is the clear bright spot, growing in users and sales.
The company returns cash to owners through a dividend and fewer shares, but it also carries a lot of debt.

earnings.headline: Apple had a record September quarter with sales of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent, though iPad and wearables sold less.
points: Sales (money coming in) were $114.5 billion, up 12 percent from a year ago. iPhone and Services set records.
Profit per share was $2.10, up 14 percent. $0.05 of that came from tariff refunds (import taxes paid back).
Worse: iPad sales fell to $6,229 million from $6,952 million. Wearables and Home fell to $8,300 million from $9,013 million.
No sales forecast (guidance) was given here. Leaders are counting on new iPhones and the all-new Siri AI for the holidays.
iPhone is the main earner: $254,098 million of $478,834 million in sales this year. Services added $123,301 million.
Spending on research rose to $45,765 million from $34,550 million. Unsold goods (inventory) jumped to $14,541 million from $5,718 million.
About 60% of sales go through other sellers, like phone carriers, rather than Apple's own stores.
Big risks they name: tariffs and trade fights, a weak economy, and relying on factories mostly in Asia for key parts.

takeaways: Apple had its best year ever for sales, mostly thanks to iPhones and Services like the App Store and iCloud.
Not everything grew: iPads and wearables sold less, and part of the profit boost came from tariff refunds.
Apple says trade fights, tariffs and supply problems in Asia could hurt the business in the future.

earnings.headline: AbbVie's sales grew and it raised its own full-year forecast, but older drugs like Humira kept shrinking.
points: Sales (revenue) were $17.404 billion, up 10.3 percent. Skyrizi ($5.776 billion) and Rinvoq ($2.706 billion) led the way.
Profit per share (EPS) was $2.37 under standard accounting rules, or $3.82 adjusted (leaving out some special costs).
Weak spots: Humira sales fell 31.2 percent, Imbruvica fell 26.1 percent, and the beauty (aesthetics) unit fell 1.4 percent.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 adjusted EPS rose to $13.95 - $13.99. The dividend goes up 5.2 percent in 2027.
AbbVie makes and sells medicines for immune diseases, brain and nerve conditions and cancer, plus beauty products like Botox.
Two drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, made up about 42% of total sales in 2025, so a lot rides on them.
Biggest risk they name: when patents (legal protection) end, cheaper copies called generics or biosimilars can cut sales fast.
They also warn that rivals and governments may challenge their patents early, which could hurt sales and earnings.
Headlines say the stock hit new 52-week highs, and one analyst firm raised its price target after the latest results.
Some articles ask what happens if Skyrizi and Rinvoq growth slows, since so much of the business depends on them.
Others debate whether the stock's price is fair compared with the company's cash flow and raised forecast.

takeaways: Most of the growth comes from two newer immune drugs, Skyrizi and Rinvoq, so the company leans heavily on them.
Older drugs like Humira and Imbruvica are shrinking fast, and cheaper copies are a risk the company names itself.

earnings.headline: Abbott's sales grew 14.5 percent, but much of that jump came from buying cancer-test maker Exact Sciences; it kept its profit forecast.
points: Sales (money coming in) rose 14.5 percent. Without the Exact Sciences purchase and currency swings, growth was 7.0 percent.
Profit per share was $0.53 by standard accounting rules, or $1.42 after removing one-off items the company excludes.
Guidance (their own forecast): full-year profit per share of $5.50 to $5.55, and sales growth of about 6.0 percent.
Weak spots: Neuromodulation sales fell 1.2 percent, and U.S. Structural Heart sales fell 11.1 percent.
Abbott sells medical devices, lab tests, baby and adult nutrition drinks, and brand-name generic drugs sold outside the U.S.
In 2025, glucose monitor sales hit $7.6 billion, up from $6.4 billion. COVID test sales fell to $297 million.
Diagnostics sales fell 4.5 percent in 2025 on weaker COVID test demand and tough conditions in China.
Risks named: tariffs, currency swings, price controls, competition, and cheaper generic drugs replacing brand ones.
Most headlines are about the stock price. One mentions trial results for the Amulet 360 heart device.

takeaways: The business grew this quarter, but a big part of the jump came from buying a cancer-testing company.
The company kept its own profit forecast steady and has raised its dividend (cash paid to owners) for 54 years in a row.
Not everything grew: some heart and nerve-device sales slipped, and nutrition sales are down 1.3 percent this year so far.

earnings.headline: Sales grew 23% to $342 million, but profit fell to $54 million from $72 million a year earlier.
points: Sales (revenue) were $342 million in the third quarter, up 23% from $279 million a year ago.
DAYBUE, a Rett syndrome drug, sold $140 million, up 39%. NUPLAZID sold $202 million, up 14%.
Profit fell: net income was $54 million, down from $72 million, as selling and office costs rose to $159 million.
Guidance (their own forecast) for 2026 DAYBUE sales rose to $505–$520 million. They also lowered their research spending forecast.
Acadia makes money selling two drugs: NUPLAZID for Parkinson's disease psychosis and DAYBUE for Rett syndrome.
Sales of the two drugs were $1,071.5 million in 2025, up from $957.8 million in 2024.
It pays partner Neuren royalties (a cut of sales) on DAYBUE, from 10% up to 15% in North America.
Big risk: copycat (generic) drugs. One legal deal lets a generic NUPLAZID launch February 27, 2038, or earlier in some cases.
The stock hit a 52-week low (its lowest price in a year) at 18.24 USD.
A court fight over NUPLAZID's patent could mean protection until 2038, or only 2030, depending on an appeal.
Other stories cover the raised sales forecast and the lower research spending forecast.

takeaways: Sales are growing, led by DAYBUE, but quarterly profit was lower than last year.
The company raised its DAYBUE forecast and had $976 million in cash and investments.
Patent fights and drug trials are the big unknowns; losing the appeal could let copycats in sooner.

points: Headlines say Organigram wants to take over Aurora. A takeover means one company buys another.
Some headlines call it a takeover battle, with Curaleaf named as a possible rival bidder. Others say Curaleaf is unlikely to bid.
One headline says Aurora's quarterly sales and profit beat what experts expected. The stock also fell on two recent days.

takeaways: Aurora may be bought by another cannabis company, Organigram. The deal is not final, and other bidders have been discussed.
Experts don't agree on this deal. Some think shareholders should accept it, while others focus on rival bidders.
These are only headlines, not the company's own reports. Wait for official filings before judging how the business is really doing.

earnings.headline: Archer moved closer to flying air taxis in LA and to closing a big Boeing deal, but it still makes almost no sales.
points: Sales: the letter gives no sales total for the quarter. The company is still mostly spending, not selling.
Profit: none yet. A cost measure (adjusted EBITDA) matched their own forecast. Money on hand: $1.4B.
Next: they expect to close buying Wisk, Insitu and SkyGrid from Boeing soon. Only one of nearly 20 approvals is left.
Surprise: the FAA cleared Midnight to start flying in LA soon. Full safety approval (type certification) is not done yet.
They make almost no money yet. The plan: sell air taxis, run air taxi rides in cities, and sell aircraft tech for defense.
They took control of Hawthorne Airport near LA and began renting hangar space. That rent is their first revenue (sales).
Losses: they lost $618.2 million in 2025 and about $2.3 billion since starting. They expect losses to continue.
Biggest risks: FAA approval may be delayed, building planes at scale is hard, and investors could lose part or all of their money.
Many headlines ask whether the stock is worth its price after it fell 46% this year.
One report says the loss got bigger this quarter. Others focus on how fast the company is spending its cash.
Writers also discuss Boeing becoming Archer's biggest shareholder once the deal closes.

takeaways: Archer is still building its product. It spends far more than it earns, and losses keep coming.
There is real progress: an FAA permit, LA flights soon, and a deal for Insitu, a drone maker with over $200 million in yearly sales.
Its big goals depend on approvals and deadlines, like the LA28 Games in 2028. The company itself warns that delays could happen.
